title: Dogen's instructions for sitting
hookLine: Dogen's short guide to zazen: sit, let go, don't think of good or bad

lines: IF THE WAY IS COMPLETE, WHY SIT?
WHAT TO DO WITH BODY AND MIND.
cards: It opens with a question that could end the whole project before it starts. If the way is already complete, everywhere, why would anyone need to practice? If it's never been lost, why sit down to find it?
That's how Dogen begins his short guide to zazen. He doesn't wave the question away. He answers with a warning: the smallest gap between you and the way, and they're as far apart as heaven and earth.
Then he tells you exactly what to do with your body and your mind.

teach.b: First, a recommendation for everyone. In Japanese the title is Fukanzazengi, rendered as a universal recommendation for zazen. Universal is the point: it's offered to everyone, not only to monks.
Second, set down every involvement. He says, in paraphrase: put aside all your involvements, let every affair rest. A quiet room, moderate food and drink, a thick mat, a cushion.
Then the posture you met earlier on this path: legs crossed or settled, hands in the oval, back upright, eyes open. Sway a little left and right, then settle into steady, unmoving sitting.
Third, non-thinking. Don't think about good or bad, he says in paraphrase; don't judge right or wrong. Stop measuring.
Then the turn. Think of not-thinking. How do you think of not-thinking?
Non-thinking. It sounds like a riddle, and readers still discuss it. One plain reading: you don't fight thoughts, and you don't follow them.
A thought arises, you notice it, and it goes on its way. Not forcing the mind blank; letting go of the grip.

teach.h: THE GATE OF EASE AND JOY.
teach.b: Fourth, the gate of ease and joy.

Zazen, Dogen says in paraphrase, isn't a technique for learning meditation. It's the gate of ease and joy, practice and awakening in one. That answers his opening question: you don't practice because the way is missing.
You practice because practice is how the way shows up.

how: Soto Zen communities chant or read Dogen's Fukanzazengi, his short guide to zazen, and teachers use it to introduce posture and the attitude of sitting without judging thoughts as good or bad.

games.q: what does “dogen's instructions for sitting” mean?
o: a guide to emptying the mind of every thought by force
a strict rulebook for monks only, kept from lay people
Dogen's short guide to zazen, recommended to everyone

p: as far apart as heaven and earth
the gate of ease and joy

s: Dogen wrote the guide only for monks
the title recommends it to everyone.
Dogen tells the sitter to force the mind blank
he says don't judge good or bad; thoughts are let go, not fought.
Dogen opens by asking why practice if the way is already complete
he raises it, then warns that the smallest gap makes heaven and earth apart.

games.q: you're sitting by Dogen's instructions. a thought comes: this sitting is going badly. what does the guide say to do?
o: fight the thought until it's gone.
don't judge good or bad; notice it and let it go.
stop sitting and try again tomorrow.
games.why: Dogen asks the sitter to stop measuring good and bad. the thought isn't fought or followed; it's let go.

practice: Settle your body, then sway gently left and right, smaller each time, until you're still, hands resting and eyes half open. Then take Dogen's instruction for the mind: when a thought comes, don't call it good or bad.
Notice it, and let it go on its way.

wordCard.voice: Dogen's instructions for sitting. His short guide to zazen: set everything down, sit upright and still, don't think of good or bad, and let thoughts go. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: Fukanzazengi, Dogen's 'universal recommendation for zazen'.

carryVoice: Your line: let go. Not a blank mind, just a looser grip. See you at the next sitting.
